chem-01.title: Matter and Atoms
explain: All the matter around us is made of tiny particles called **atoms**. An atom consists of a **nucleus** at its center and **electrons** that move around it. Inside the nucleus are **protons** and **neutrons**.

- Proton: charge +, located in the nucleus.
- Neutron: no charge (neutral), located in the nucleus.
- Electron: charge −, located outside the nucleus.

explain: The number of **protons** in an atom is called the **atomic number**. Atoms with the same atomic number are the same **element**, and each element has its own unique number. An atom in its normal state has zero net charge, so its number of protons equals its number of electrons.

The sum of the number of protons and the number of neutrons is the **mass number**. The lithium in the figure has 3 protons and 4 neutrons, so its mass number is 7. That is why it is called lithium-7.

chem-02.title: The Periodic Table
explain: The **periodic table** arranges the elements in order of atomic number so that elements with similar properties fall in the same vertical column. The horizontal rows are called **periods**, and the vertical columns are called **groups**. Periods are numbered 1 to 7, and groups are numbered 1 to 18.

explain:
Elements in the same group have similar chemical properties. Three representative groups are as follows.
- Group 1 alkali metals (Li, Na, K, etc.): soft metals that react vigorously with water.
- Group 17 halogens (F, Cl, etc.): easily combine with other elements.
- Group 18 noble gases (He, Ne, Ar, etc.): hardly react with other elements.

How to read the table: moving from left to right increases the atomic number by 1 at each step. When a row ends, you move on to the next period. Period 1 contains only H and He, while periods 2 and 3 each contain 8 elements.

chem-03.title: Chemical Bonds
explain: Atoms combine with one another to form substances; this is called **bonding**. The key to understanding bonding is the outermost electrons, called **valence electrons**. Noble gases in group 18 have a stable arrangement of valence electrons, so they rarely react. Other atoms tend to move toward this stable arrangement by transferring electrons to or from one another, or by sharing them.

**Ionic bond**: One atom gives up an electron and another atom accepts it. The atom that gave up an electron becomes a **cation** with a + charge, and the atom that accepted it becomes an **anion** with a − charge. The two are held together by electrostatic attraction. Table salt (NaCl) is a typical example.

explain.alt: At the top, before electron transfer, Na has 1 valence electron and Cl has 7 valence electrons, with an arrow showing one electron moving from Na to Cl. At the bottom, after the transfer, Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are shown touching, labeled as held together by electrostatic attraction (ionic bond).
explain.caption: One electron moves from Na to Cl, forming Na⁺ and Cl⁻.

explain: **Covalent bond**: Atoms share electrons with one another. A pair of electrons shared in this way is called a **shared electron pair**. In water (H₂O), the O atom shares one electron pair with each of the two H atoms. A particle formed by a covalent bond is called a **molecule**.

Labels on both sides point to these electron pairs as shared electron pairs. Below, it is written that one O shares one electron pair with each of two H atoms (H₂O).
explain.caption: A water molecule. It has two shared electron pairs.

explain: In general, ionic bonds are common between metals and nonmetals, and covalent bonds are common between nonmetals. There are exceptions, however, so treat this as a tendency rather than a rule.

chem-04.title: Chemical Equations
explain: In a **chemical reaction**, atoms form new pairings and become different substances. The substances before the reaction are called **reactants**, and the substances after the reaction are called **products**. Writing a reaction in chemical formulas is called a **chemical equation**.

In a chemical reaction, atoms are neither created nor destroyed; only their pairings change. Therefore, the kinds and numbers of atoms are the same before and after the reaction, and so is the total mass. This is the **law of conservation of mass**. In a chemical equation, a **coefficient** is placed in front of a formula to make the number of atoms on each side equal. A coefficient of 1 is not written. Subscripts within a formula are never changed.

chem-05.title: Introduction to the Mole
explain: Atoms and molecules are too small and too numerous to count one by one. So chemistry uses a very large counting unit, the **mole** (mol), just as a dozen is a group of 12. One mole is $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ particles.

The mass in grams of one mole of atoms equals the value of its atomic mass. The atomic masses used in this lesson are H = 1, C = 12, and O = 16. The mass of one mole of a molecule is the sum of the atomic masses of the atoms that make it up. This is the **molar mass** $M$ (unit: g/mol).
$$\text{물질의 양(mol)} = \dfrac{\text{질량(g)}}{\text{몰질량(g/mol)}}$$

chem-06.title: Acids and Bases
explain: The most basic definition is that a substance that releases **hydrogen ions** (H⁺) when dissolved in water is called an **acid**, and a substance that releases **hydroxide ions** (OH⁻) when dissolved in water is called a **base**. The sour taste of vinegar or lemon juice comes from acids, and the slipperiness of soap is related to bases. Do not taste or touch unfamiliar substances. Here we deal only with the concepts.
How acidic an aqueous solution is, is expressed by its **pH**. A scale from 0 to 14 is usually used, with 7 being neutral. Values below 7 are acidic, and values above 7 are basic.

explain.alt: A pH scale with 15 divisions from 0 to 14. 0 to 6 is marked as acidic, 7 is neutral, and 8 to 14 is basic, with the colors gradually changing. Below the scale, lemon juice is about 2, coffee about 5, pure water 7, and household ammonia water about 11. At the bottom it is written that each decrease of 1 means 10 times more hydrogen ions.
explain.caption: The pH scale and a few examples. The values are approximate.

explain: When the pH decreases by 1, the amount of hydrogen ions becomes **10 times** larger. So a solution with pH 3 has 10 times as many hydrogen ions as a solution with pH 4, and 100 times as many as a solution with pH 5.

When an acid and a base meet, a **neutralization reaction** occurs in which each weakens the other's properties, producing water and a **salt**. The name resembles table salt, but 'salt' is a general term for the ionic compounds produced in such reactions.

chem-07.title: Reaction Heat and Enthalpy: Hess's Law
explain: Burning fuel releases heat, and a cold pack gets cold when its pouch is broken. Chemical reactions almost always involve the absorption or release of heat. However, some reaction heats are very difficult to measure directly. For example, it is practically impossible to stop the burning of carbon exactly at carbon monoxide. Chemical thermodynamics provides a way to **calculate reaction heats that cannot be measured directly from reaction heats that can be measured**.

The heat absorbed by a system at constant pressure is called the **enthalpy change** $\Delta H$. If $\Delta H < 0$, the reaction is **exothermic**, releasing heat; if $\Delta H > 0$, it is **endothermic**, absorbing heat. Enthalpy is a **state function**. Just as the difference in altitude between two points does not depend on which route was taken, $\Delta H$ is determined only by the initial and final states.

This property directly leads to **Hess's law**. Even if a reaction proceeds in several steps, the total $\Delta H$ equals the sum of the $\Delta H$ values of the steps. Reversing a reaction equation changes the sign, and multiplying all coefficients by $n$ multiplies $\Delta H$ by $n$. To obtain the target reaction, add and subtract the reaction equations as if they were algebraic equations.

explain.alt: Hess cycle diagram. An arrow goes directly from the upper left box C(s) + O₂(g) to the upper right box CO₂(g), labeled ΔH = −393.5 kJ. The other path passes through the lower box CO(g) + ½O₂(g): the first arrow is labeled ΔH₁ = ?, and the second arrow is labeled ΔH₂ = −283.0 kJ.

explain: The enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states (1 bar, usually 25°C) is called the **standard enthalpy of formation** $\Delta H_f^\circ$. By definition, the most stable form of an element has a value of 0. Then the enthalpy change of any reaction can be calculated as $$\Delta H^\circ_{반응} = \sum n\,\Delta H_f^\circ(\text{생성물}) - \sum n\,\Delta H_f^\circ(\text{반응물})$$ This is equivalent to the Hess path in which the reactants are first decomposed into elements and then reassembled into the products.

**Bond enthalpy** can also be used for an estimate. Breaking bonds requires energy, and forming bonds releases energy, so $\Delta H \approx \sum(\text{끊는 결합}) - \sum(\text{만드는 결합})$. However, bond enthalpy tables give **average values** over many molecules, so this method is an approximation. A value calculated from formation enthalpies is more accurate.

Limitation: $\Delta H$ only tells you **how much heat** a reaction releases or absorbs; it does not tell you whether the reaction occurs **spontaneously**. For example, the endothermic melting of ice also occurs spontaneously at room temperature. To judge spontaneity, we need entropy and Gibbs free energy, covered in the next lesson.

examples.title: The Hess Cycle in the Figure
body: Given: C + O₂ → CO₂ ($-393.5$ kJ), CO + ½O₂ → CO₂ ($-283.0$ kJ). Target: $\Delta H_1$ for C + ½O₂ → CO.
Step 1: The two paths must give the same total, so $\Delta H_1 + (-283.0) = -393.5$.
Step 2: $\Delta H_1 = -110.5$ kJ. We obtained a reaction heat that is hard to measure directly from two measurable combustion heats.

examples.title: Calculating Combustion Heat from Enthalpies of Formation
body: Given: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O(l). $\Delta H_f^\circ$: CH₄ $-74.8$, CO₂ $-393.5$, H₂O(l) $-285.8$ kJ/mol, O₂ 0.
Step 1: Sum for the products $= -393.5 + 2(-285.8) = -965.1$. Sum for the reactants $= -74.8$.
Step 2: $\Delta H^\circ = -965.1 - (-74.8) = -890.3$ kJ/mol. If the coefficient 2 is left out, you get about 285 kJ, which is incorrect.

chem-08.title: Entropy and Gibbs Free Energy: Spontaneity
explain: As seen in the previous lesson, not only exothermic reactions occur spontaneously. Ice absorbs heat as it melts, and ammonium nitrate dissolves in water and cools its surroundings. Spontaneity has another factor besides energy. That factor is **entropy**.

Entropy $S$ is a quantity that represents the number of microstates a system can have (as covered in the stage 3 physics lessons: $S = k_B\ln\Omega$). In chemistry, it is enough to remember the following tendencies. Entropy increases in the order solid < liquid < gas; **reactions that increase the number of gas molecules** increase entropy; and dissolution, mixing, and rising temperature generally increase entropy as well. Using standard molar entropies $S^\circ$, we obtain $\Delta S^\circ = \sum nS^\circ(\text{생성물}) - \sum nS^\circ(\text{반응물})$.

The second law of thermodynamics says that changes occur in the direction in which the entropy of the universe (system + surroundings) increases. At constant temperature and pressure, when the system releases heat $\Delta H$, the entropy of the surroundings changes by $-\Delta H/T$. Therefore $\Delta S_{우주} = \Delta S - \Delta H/T$, and multiplying both sides by $-T$ gives the change in **Gibbs free energy**, written in terms of the system alone: $$\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$$ 일정 온도·압력에서 $\Delta G < 0$이면 자발적, $\Delta G > 0$이면 비자발적, $\Delta G = 0$ means equilibrium.

Four cases arise from the sign combinations of $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$. ① $\Delta H < 0$, $\Delta S > 0$: spontaneous at all temperatures. ② $\Delta H > 0$, $\Delta S < 0$: nonspontaneous at all temperatures. ③ $\Delta H < 0$, $\Delta S < 0$: spontaneous **only at low temperatures**. ④ $\Delta H > 0$, $\Delta S > 0$: spontaneous **only at high temperatures**. In cases ③ and ④, the temperature at which spontaneity switches is $T = \Delta H/\Delta S$.

Melting of ice is an example of case ④. With $\Delta H = +6.01$ kJ/mol and $\Delta S = +22.0$ J/(mol·K), $T = 6010/22.0 \approx 273$ K, so the system is at equilibrium at 0°C and melts at higher temperatures. Be careful with units. $\Delta H$ is usually given in kJ and $\Delta S$ in J, so the units must be matched before calculating.

Limitation: $\Delta G < 0$ means a reaction **can occur**, not that it occurs **quickly**. For example, the conversion of diamond to graphite has $\Delta G < 0$ at room temperature, but it practically does not occur. Reaction speed belongs to the domain of chemical kinetics in stage 4. Also, the assumption that $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ hardly change with temperature is only an approximation over a wide temperature range.

examples.title: The Temperature at Which Spontaneity Changes
body: Given: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g). $\Delta H^\circ = +178$ kJ, $\Delta S^\circ = +161$ J/K.
Step 1 (25°C): $\Delta G^\circ = 178 - 298 \times 0.161 \approx 130$ kJ $> 0$. Nonspontaneous.

Step 2: The temperature at which spontaneity switches is $T = 178000/161 \approx 1106$ K (about 833°C). This is why the kiln must be hotter than this to produce lime. Because a gas is produced, $\Delta S > 0$.

chem-09.title: Chemical Equilibrium and the Equilibrium Constant: Le Châtelier's Principle
explain: Most reactions do not proceed until the reactants are all used up. Forward and reverse reactions occur together, and when their rates become equal, the concentrations stop changing; this is a **dynamic equilibrium**. Even at equilibrium, molecules continue to react. The rates in both directions are simply equal.

For the equilibrium of the reaction $a\text{A} + b\text{B} \rightleftharpoons c\text{C} + d\text{D}$, at a given temperature, regardless of the initial concentrations, $$K = \frac{[\text{C}]^c[\text{D}]^d}{[\text{A}]^a[\text{B}]^b}$$ 가 일정하다(**질량작용 법칙**). 순수한 고체와 액체는 식에 넣지 않는다. $K \gg 1$이면 평형이 생성물 쪽에, $K \ll 1$, it lies toward the reactants.

The value calculated with the same expression at a moment when the system is not at equilibrium is called the **reaction quotient** $Q$. If $Q < K$, there are too few products and the reaction proceeds in the forward direction; if $Q > K$, it proceeds in the reverse direction. Comparing $Q$ and $K$ is a quantitative way to answer the question 'which way will it go?'

The equilibrium constant is connected to the free energy of the previous lesson. We have $\Delta G = \Delta G^\circ + RT\ln Q$, and at equilibrium $\Delta G = 0$ and $Q = K$, so $$\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K$$ 이다. $\Delta G^\circ$가 음수로 클수록 $K$는 지수적으로 커진다. 25°C에서 $\Delta G^\circ$가 약 5.7 kJ 줄 때마다 $K$ by a factor of 10.

**Le Châtelier's principle**: When a change is applied to a system at equilibrium, the system shifts its equilibrium in the direction that reduces the effect of that change. Adding a reactant shifts the equilibrium toward the forward direction, and increasing pressure shifts it toward the side with fewer moles of gas. Raising the temperature of an exothermic reaction shifts it toward the reverse direction, and in this case **$K$ itself changes**. Changes in concentration or pressure do not change $K$; they only change $Q$. A catalyst increases the rate at which equilibrium is reached but does not change the equilibrium position.

Limitation: The $K$ written with concentrations is accurate for dilute solutions and low-pressure ideal cases. For concentrated solutions, it must be rewritten using **activities**. Also, Le Châtelier's principle tells only the direction; to know how far the equilibrium shifts, you must calculate with $K$.

examples.title: Judging the Direction Using Q
body: Given: H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI, with $K = 50$ at a certain temperature. Current concentrations: [H₂] = 0.1, [I₂] = 0.1, [HI] = 0.5 M.
Step 2: Since $Q < K$, the reaction proceeds in the forward direction, producing more HI.

chem-10.title: Weak Acid Equilibria and pH
explain: In stage 1, we learned that acids are substances that release hydrogen ions. However, even at the same 0.1 M concentration, hydrochloric acid has a pH of 1, while the acetic acid in vinegar has a pH of about 2.9. This difference comes from **how completely** the acid ionizes. Ionization of a weak acid is an equilibrium, and it can be handled with the equilibrium constant learned in stage 2.

For the ionization of a weak acid HA, $\text{HA} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{A}^-$, the equilibrium constant is called the **acid dissociation constant** $K_a = \frac{[\text{H}^+][\text{A}^-]}{[\text{HA}]}$. The larger $K_a$ is, the stronger the acid. For convenience, $\text{p}K_a = -\log K_a$ is used, and the **smaller** $\text{p}K_a$ is, the stronger the acid. For acetic acid, $K_a = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}$ and $\text{p}K_a \approx 4.74$.

Let us find the pH of a weak acid of concentration $C$. If the amount ionized is $x$, then $K_a = \frac{x^2}{C - x}$. Since a weak acid ionizes very little, approximating $C - x \approx C$ gives $x = \sqrt{K_aC}$, that is, $$[\text{H}^+] \approx \sqrt{K_aC}$$ 이다. 근사가 타당한지는 $x/C$가 5% 미만인지로 확인한다. 0.1 M 아세트산은 $[\text{H}^+] \approx 1.34 \times 10^{-3}$ M, pH $\approx 2.87$, and the fraction ionized is about 1.3%.

For an acid and its conjugate base, $K_a \times K_b = K_w = 1.0 \times 10^{-14}$ (25°C) holds. **The conjugate base of a strong acid is very weak**, while the conjugate base of a weak acid is somewhat basic. Thus an aqueous solution of sodium acetate is weakly basic. This fact explains why the equivalence-point pH in the titrations covered in the next lesson is not 7.

Water itself also ionizes slightly, as $\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{OH}^-$, and $[\text{H}^+][\text{OH}^-] = K_w$. Therefore at 25°C, $\text{pH} + \text{pOH} = 14$. Since $K_w$ changes with temperature, near body temperature the pH of a neutral solution is slightly below 7.

Limitation: The approximation $\sqrt{K_aC}$ breaks down when the acid is very dilute or $K_a$ is large. If you calculate the pH of $10^{-8}$ M hydrochloric acid as 8, you get the contradiction of an acid that is basic. At this dilution, the $\text{H}^+$ coming from the ionization of water cannot be ignored.

chem-11.title: Buffer Solutions and Titration Curves
explain: The pH of blood is kept within a very narrow range, about 7.4. Even when a small amount of acidic substance enters, the pH barely changes. A solution that resists changes in pH in this way is called a **buffer solution**, and it is made by mixing a weak acid with its conjugate base (or a weak base with its conjugate acid).

The principle of buffering is simple. When a strong acid enters, the conjugate base $\text{A}^-$ accepts the $\text{H}^+$ and becomes HA; when a strong base enters, HA neutralizes the $\text{OH}^-$ and becomes $\text{A}^-$. Because strong acids and bases are "exchanged" for weak ones, the change in pH is small. Taking the logarithm of the $K_a$ expression gives the **Henderson–Hasselbalch equation**: $$\text{pH} = \text{p}K_a + \log\frac{[\text{A}^-]}{[\text{HA}]}$$

Two things can be read directly from this equation. ① If $[\text{A}^-] = [\text{HA}]$, then $\text{pH} = \text{p}K_a$. ② The pH changes by 1 only when the ratio changes tenfold. Therefore the buffering capacity is best in the range $\text{pH} \approx \text{p}K_a \pm 1$, so you should choose an acid whose $\text{p}K_a$ is close to the desired pH.

explain.alt: Titration curve. The horizontal axis is the volume of NaOH added (mL, 0 to 50), and the vertical axis is pH (0 to 14). 25 mL of 0.1 M weak acid is titrated with 0.1 M NaOH. The pH starts at about 2.9, rises gently, jumps sharply near 25 mL, and then stays at about 12. Point A, at 12.5 mL, is at pH about 4.8, and point B, at 25 mL, is at pH about 8.7.

explain: A **titration curve** is a record of pH as a base is added little by little to an acid. The figure shows a weak acid titrated with a strong base. At first only the weak acid is present, so the pH is about 2.9. When base is added, a buffer region containing both HA and A⁻ forms, and the pH rises gently. At the **half-equivalence point** (point A), where the amount of base added is half that of the original acid, $[\text{HA}] = [\text{A}^-]$, so **pH = p$K_a$**. This is how a titration curve can be used to measure $\text{p}K_a$.

At the **equivalence point** (point B), where all the acid has been neutralized, only the conjugate base $\text{A}^-$ remains in the solution, so the solution is **weakly basic** (pH ≈ 8.7), as seen in the previous lesson. This differs from the equivalence point of a strong acid–strong base titration, which is pH 7. That is why an indicator is chosen whose color changes near the equivalence point (in this case, phenolphthalein). Beyond the equivalence point, the excess strong base determines the pH.

examples.title: The pH of a Buffer and the Addition of Acid
body: Given: a 1 L solution containing 0.10 mol of acetic acid and 0.10 mol of sodium acetate, $\text{p}K_a = 4.74$.
Step 1: The ratio is 1, so pH = 4.74.
Step 2: If 0.01 mol of HCl is added, A⁻ becomes 0.09 mol and HA becomes 0.11 mol. pH $= 4.74 + \log(0.09/0.11) \approx 4.65$. Had this been 1 L of pure water, the pH would have dropped from 7 to 2.

chem-12.title: Solubility Product and Electrochemistry: Electromotive Force and Free Energy
explain: Equilibrium constants are not limited to acids and bases. The extent to which a poorly soluble salt dissolves, and the voltage a battery produces, can both be described in the language of equilibrium and free energy. This lesson covers two applications of solution equilibria: the **solubility product** and **electrochemistry**.

For a sparingly soluble salt $\text{M}_a\text{X}_b(s) \rightleftharpoons a\text{M}^{n+} + b\text{X}^{m-}$, the equilibrium constant is called the **solubility product** $K_{sp} = [\text{M}]^a[\text{X}]^b$ (solids are not included in the expression). If the molar solubility is $s$, then for a 1:1 salt such as AgCl, $K_{sp} = s^2$, and for a 1:2 salt such as CaF₂, $K_{sp} = s(2s)^2 = 4s^3$. If **the same ion** is already present, the solubility decreases according to Le Châtelier's principle (the common-ion effect). If the ion product $Q > K_{sp}$, a precipitate forms.

In an **oxidation–reduction reaction**, electrons are transferred. If oxidation (loss of electrons) and reduction (gain of electrons) are separated into two compartments and connected by a wire, electrons flow through the wire, forming a **galvanic cell**. The electrode where oxidation occurs is the **anode**, and the electrode where reduction occurs is the **cathode**. The tendency of each half-reaction, measured relative to the hydrogen electrode, is its **standard reduction potential** $E^\circ$.

The standard electromotive force of a cell is $E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ_{환원전극} - E^\circ_{산화전극}$. The species with the larger $E^\circ$ is reduced. For example, Cu²⁺/Cu is $+0.34$ V and Zn²⁺/Zn is $-0.76$ V, so the electromotive force of the Daniell cell is $0.34 - (-0.76) = 1.10$ V. Even when a half-reaction is multiplied by a coefficient, $E^\circ$ is **not multiplied**, because a potential is the energy per electron.

Electrochemistry is directly connected to free energy. The maximum electrical work that $n$ moles of electrons can perform while passing through an electromotive force $E$ is $nFE$ ($F = 96{,}485$ C/mol, the Faraday constant), and $$\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ_{cell}$$ 이다. $E^\circ > 0$이면 $\Delta G^\circ < 0$, 즉 자발적이다. 2단계의 $\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K$ from stage 2, the equilibrium constant can be found from the electromotive force.

Limitation: Standard potentials are values under standard conditions in which all concentrations are 1 M. Real cells have changing concentrations, and their electromotive force decreases (the Nernst equation). Also, even if $E^\circ$ is large, if the reaction at the electrode surface is slow, the actual current may be small. The principle holds here as well: thermodynamics tells us what is possible, and kinetics tells us the actual rate.

chem-13.title: Rate Laws and Reaction Order
explain: Stage 2 thermodynamics tells us **in which direction and how far** a reaction goes, but not **how fast** it goes. Turning diamond into graphite takes billions of years, while an explosion happens in an instant. **Chemical kinetics** deals with reaction speed quantitatively.

The reaction rate is the change in concentration per unit time. For $a\text{A} \to$ products, the rate is $= -\frac{1}{a}\frac{d[\text{A}]}{dt}$, dividing by the coefficient so that the same value results no matter which substance is used to measure it. The rate usually depends on concentrations and is written as the experimentally determined **rate law** $$\text{속도} = k[\text{A}]^m[\text{B}]^n$$ 으로 쓴다. $k$는 **속도 상수**, $m, n$은 각 물질에 대한 **반응 차수**, $m + n$ is the overall order.

The most important caution: **reaction orders are unrelated to the coefficients in the reaction equation and can be determined only by experiment.** The rate law for 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂ happens to be $k[\text{NO}]^2[\text{O}_2]$, but many reactions, such as those of the H₂ + I₂ → 2HI type, differ from what the coefficients alone would predict. Orders reflect the actual pathway of the reaction (its mechanism).

The standard method for determining orders is the **initial rate method**. Change the initial concentration of only one substance, keep the others fixed, and measure the initial rate. If doubling [A] leaves the rate unchanged, the order is 0; if it doubles the rate, the order is 1; if it quadruples the rate, the order is 2. In general, for a concentration ratio $c$, the rate ratio is $c^m$, so $m = \log(\text{속도 비})/\log(c)$.

Once the orders are determined, the units of $k$ are also determined. Since the unit of rate is M/s, the $k$ of a first-order reaction is s⁻¹, and the $k$ of a second-order reaction is M⁻¹s⁻¹. By looking at the units of $k$, you can work backward to the reaction order.

Limitation: The rate law is reliable only within the ranges of concentration and temperature where it was measured. Some reactions, such as enzyme reactions, change behavior: they are first order at low concentrations and zero order at high concentrations (Michaelis–Menten). Also, a simple rate law holds only if rates are measured in the **initial** stage, far from equilibrium, where the reverse reaction is negligible.

examples.title: Determining Orders by the Initial Rate Method
body: Given: Experiment 1 [A] = 0.1, [B] = 0.1, rate 2.0×10⁻³ / Experiment 2 [A] = 0.2, [B] = 0.1, rate 8.0×10⁻³ / Experiment 3 [A] = 0.1, [B] = 0.3, rate 6.0×10⁻³ (M/s).
Step 1: From 1 to 2, [A] doubles and the rate quadruples, so the reaction is second order in A. From 1 to 3, [B] triples and the rate triples, so the reaction is first order in B.
Step 2: Rate $= k[\text{A}]^2[\text{B}]$. From experiment 1, $k = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}/(0.01 \times 0.1) = 2.0$ M⁻²s⁻¹. The overall reaction is third order.

Interpretation: For rate (M/s) $= k \times$ (M)$^n$ to hold, $n = 2$. The overall reaction is second order.

chem-14.title: Integrated Rate Laws and Half-Life
explain: A rate law tells us "how fast right now." But what we really want to know is "how much will remain after 10 minutes?" and "how long will it take for half to disappear?" Integrating the rate law with respect to time gives the **integrated rate law**, which answers these questions. The first-order differential equation from the stage 5 mathematics course is used directly.

The **first-order reaction** $-\frac{d[\text{A}]}{dt} = k[\text{A}]$ separates to $\ln[\text{A}] = \ln[\text{A}]_0 - kt$, that is, $[\text{A}] = [\text{A}]_0e^{-kt}$. **A plot of $\ln[\text{A}]$ against $t$ is a straight line with slope $-k$.** The half-life is $t_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{k} \approx \frac{0.693}{k}$, which is **independent of the initial concentration**. Radioactive decay is a typical first-order process.

explain.alt: Graph with time t (minutes, 0 to 30) on the horizontal axis and ln[A] on the vertical axis. A straight line passing through the points (0, 0), (10, −1.0), (20, −2.0), and (30, −3.0) is drawn.

explain: The **second-order reaction** $-\frac{d[\text{A}]}{dt} = k[\text{A}]^2$ gives $\frac{1}{[\text{A}]} = \frac{1}{[\text{A}]_0} + kt$, so a plot of $1/[\text{A}]$ against $t$ is a straight line. The half-life $t_{1/2} = \frac{1}{k[\text{A}]_0}$ is inversely proportional to the initial concentration, so each successive half-life becomes longer as the reaction proceeds. The **zero-order reaction** has $[\text{A}] = [\text{A}]_0 - kt$, so the concentration itself decreases linearly; its half-life $[\text{A}]_0/2k$ is proportional to the initial concentration.

This is the second method for determining orders from experimental data, the **graphical method**. Plot the concentration data against time as $[\text{A}]$, $\ln[\text{A}]$, and $1/[\text{A}]$, and find the one that gives a **straight line**. The graph that is linear reveals the order, and its slope gives $k$.

Limitation: For reactions involving several steps, or reactions in which the reverse reaction cannot be neglected, no graph will be perfectly straight. Also, if the measurement interval is too short (observing only part of a half-life), the first- and second-order graphs both look nearly straight, making them hard to tell apart. Data spanning at least two or three half-lives are needed.

examples.title: k and the Half-Life from a Graph
body: Given: the $\ln[\text{A}]$ line in the figure, which passes through (0, 0) and (20, −2.0).
Step 1: Slope $= -2.0/20 = -0.1$ min⁻¹, so $k = 0.1$ min⁻¹. Since the plot is a straight line, the reaction is first order.
Step 2: $t_{1/2} = 0.693/0.1 \approx 6.9$ min. The fraction remaining after 30 minutes is $e^{-3} \approx 0.050$, that is, 5%.

examples.title: Half-Life of a Second-Order Reaction
body: Given: $2\text{NO}_2 \to 2\text{NO} + \text{O}_2$ is second order, $k = 0.5$ M⁻¹s⁻¹, $[\text{A}]_0 = 0.2$ M.
Step 1: The first half-life $= 1/(0.5 \times 0.2) = 10$ s.
Step 2: After the concentration reaches 0.1 M, the next half-life is $1/(0.5 \times 0.1) = 20$ s. The doubling of the half-life is the signature of a second-order reaction.

chem-15.title: The Arrhenius Equation, Catalysts, and Reaction Mechanisms
explain: Putting food in a refrigerator slows the rate at which it spoils, and cooking over a strong flame makes it cook faster. Most reactions speed up two- to threefold for every 10°C rise in temperature. The **activation energy** explains why temperature has such a large effect and how a catalyst speeds up a reaction.

For a reaction to occur, molecules must collide with enough energy to rearrange their bonds. The minimum energy needed to reach the top of the energy barrier between reactants and products, the **transition state**, is the **activation energy** $E_a$. Arrhenius found that the rate constant follows $$k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}$$ 를 따른다는 것을 발견했다. 지수 인자 $e^{-E_a/RT}$는 $E_a$.

explain.alt: Reaction energy diagram. The vertical axis (energy in kJ/mol) has tick marks at 0, −40, 50, and 80. The reactants are at 0 and the products are at −40. Solid path ① peaks at 80, and dashed path ② peaks at 50; both go from the same reactants to the same products.

explain: The activation energy $E_a$ can be obtained from rate constants measured at two temperatures: $$\ln\frac{k_2}{k_1} = \frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_1} - \frac{1}{T_2}\right)$$ 또는 $\ln k$ 대 $1/T$를 그리면 기울기 $-E_a/R$인 직선(아레니우스 도표)이 된다. $E_a$ is, the more sensitive the rate is to temperature.

A **catalyst** provides a **different pathway** with a lower activation energy. The dashed path in the figure is such a pathway. Since the energies of the reactants and products are unchanged, $\Delta H$ and the equilibrium constant do not change, and the forward and reverse reactions speed up **by the same ratio**. Enzymes are biological catalysts; they greatly lower the activation energy so that reactions proceed rapidly even at body temperature.

Many reactions consist of several **elementary steps**. The sequence of these steps is the **reaction mechanism**. In an elementary step, the coefficient is the order. The slowest of the steps, the **rate-determining step**, determines the overall rate. For example, NO₂ + CO → NO + CO₂ proceeds through step 1, NO₂ + NO₂ → NO₃ + NO (slow), and step 2, NO₃ + CO → NO₂ + CO₂ (fast), so the rate law becomes $k[\text{NO}_2]^2$, independent of CO. The intermediate NO₃ does not appear in the overall reaction equation.

Limitation: A mechanism can be shown to be **consistent with** the experimental rate law, but it cannot be proven. Different mechanisms may give the same rate law. Also, treating $A$ and $E_a$ in the Arrhenius equation as constants is an approximation over a narrow temperature range.

examples.title: Reading an Energy Diagram
body: Given: the figure. Reactants 0, products −40, path ① peak 80, path ② peak 50 kJ/mol.
Step 1: $\Delta H = -40$ kJ/mol (exothermic). $E_a$ is 80 for path ① and 50 kJ/mol for path ②.
Step 2: The activation energy of the reverse reaction runs from the products to the peak, so it is 120 for path ① and 90 kJ/mol for path ②. The catalyst lowered it by 30 kJ in both directions.

Step 2: $E_a \approx 0.693 \times 8.314 / 1.075 \times 10^{-4} \approx 53.6$ kJ/mol. The rule of thumb that the rate doubles per 10 degrees corresponds roughly to an $E_a$ of this size.

chem-16.title: Hybrid Orbitals and Molecular Shape
explain: The four C–H bonds in methane, CH₄, are all identical and arranged in a tetrahedron with 109.5° between them. Yet the valence electrons of carbon are arranged differently: 2 in the 2s orbital and 2 in the 2p orbitals. How can different orbitals form four identical bonds? The concept of **hybrid orbitals**, the starting point of organic chemistry, answers this question.

**Hybridization** is mixing the s and p orbitals of the same atom to make new equivalent orbitals. Mixing one s and three p orbitals gives four **sp³** orbitals pointing in tetrahedral directions (109.5°). One s and two p orbitals give three **sp²** orbitals in a flat triangle (120°), while the remaining p orbital stands perpendicular to that plane. One s and one p orbital give two **sp** orbitals in a straight line (180°), leaving two p orbitals.

There are two kinds of bonds. When orbitals overlap head-on along the axis joining the two nuclei, it is a **σ (sigma) bond**; when parallel p orbitals overlap sideways, it is a **π (pi) bond**. A single bond has one σ; a double bond has one σ and one π; a triple bond has one σ and two π. The carbons in ethylene (C=C) are sp², and the carbons in acetylene (C≡C) are sp.

A practical rule: the **steric number**, which is the number of atoms bonded to the central atom plus the number of lone pairs, is 4 for sp³, 3 for sp², and 2 for sp. This gives the same result as the valence-shell electron-pair repulsion (VSEPR) principle from stage 1. The oxygen in water, H₂O, has 2 bonds and 2 lone pairs, a steric number of 4, and so is sp³; but because the lone pairs push more strongly, the bond angle shrinks to about 104.5°.

A π bond prevents rotation. A single bond can rotate freely about its axis, but in a double bond, rotation breaks the sideways overlap of the p orbitals. Therefore 2-butene has **cis–trans isomers**, which have the same order of atomic connections but different shapes and do not readily interconvert. This leads into the stereochemistry of the next lesson.

Limitation: Hybrid orbitals are a very useful model for describing molecular shapes, but they are an approximation of the actual electronic structure. For cases where electrons are spread over several atoms, such as benzene, molecular orbital theory is more accurate. It is also safer to regard hybridization as a language for **describing** observed shapes, rather than as the **cause** that predicts them.

examples.title: Determining the Hybridization of Carbons in a Molecule
body: Given: acetaldehyde, CH₃-CHO.
Step 1: The carbon in CH₃ is bonded to 4 atoms, so its steric number is 4 → sp³, about 109.5°.
Step 2: The carbon in CHO is bonded to H, CH₃, and O (double bond), so its steric number is 3 → sp², about 120°. The C=O contains one σ and one π.

Step 1: C–H 6 bonds (σ 6), C–C single bond 1 (σ 1), C=C 1 (σ 1 + π 1).
Step 2: 8 σ bonds and 1 π bond in total. The two carbons of the double bond are sp², and the terminal CH₃ carbon is sp³.

chem-17.title: Stereoisomers and Chirality
explain: Left and right hands have the same arrangement of fingers, but no matter how you turn them, they cannot be superimposed. Molecules also have this kind of handedness. Molecules that have the same sequence of atomic connections but differ only in their spatial arrangement are called **stereoisomers**, and this difference can completely change a drug's effect, a fragrance, or a taste.

A molecule that cannot be superimposed on its mirror image is called **chiral**. The most common cause is an **sp³ carbon bonded to four different atoms or groups**, that is, a **stereocenter** (chiral center). A pair of isomers that are mirror images of each other is called **enantiomers**. If a molecule has a plane of symmetry, it is not chiral.

Enantiomers have **the same** values for most physical properties, such as melting point, boiling point, and solubility. They differ in two ways. ① They rotate plane-polarized light by **the same angle in opposite directions** (optical activity). A **racemic mixture**, in which the two enantiomers are present 1:1, has no optical activity because the rotations cancel. ② They react differently with **other chiral molecules**. Enzymes and receptors in the body are chiral, so enantiomers can have different physiological effects.

The arrangement at a stereocenter is expressed with the **R/S notation** (Cahn–Ingold–Prelog rules). ① Assign priorities 1 to 4 to the four substituents in order of decreasing atomic number; if the first atoms are the same, compare the next atoms. ② Place the group with priority 4 (the lowest) away from the viewer. ③ If 1 → 2 → 3 runs clockwise, the center is **R**; if counterclockwise, it is **S**. R/S is only the name of the arrangement and is separate from the direction of optical rotation (+/−).

If there are $n$ stereocenters, there are at most $2^n$ stereoisomers. When there are two or more stereocenters, **diastereomers**, stereoisomers that are **not** mirror images, can arise, and they have different physical properties. Also, a **meso compound** may be achiral because of an internal plane of symmetry despite having stereocenters, so the actual number may be less than $2^n$.

Limitation: Some molecules are chiral without a stereocenter (for example, allenes with axial chirality), and some molecules with stereocenters are achiral (meso compounds). 'Stereocenter = chiral' is a convenient rule of thumb, not a definition. The definition is whether the molecule can be superimposed on its mirror image.

examples.title: Finding a Stereocenter
body: Given: 2-butanol, CH₃-CH(OH)-CH₂-CH₃.
Step 1: The second carbon bears four different groups: H, OH, CH₃, and CH₂CH₃. It is a stereocenter.
Step 2: Therefore there are two enantiomers, R and S. 1-Butanol (with CH₂OH at the end) has no stereocenter, because its carbons each have two identical H atoms.

Step 1: Compare the atomic numbers of the first atoms: O (8) > C (6) = C (6) > H (1). OH is 1, and H is 4.
Step 2: To compare the two C atoms, look at the next atoms. CH₃ is (H, H, H) and CH₂CH₃ is (C, H, H), so ethyl is 2 and methyl is 3.

chem-18.title: Nucleophilic Substitution, Elimination, and Infrared Spectroscopy
explain: Organic synthesis is the work of attaching a desired functional group at a desired position. The basic tool for this is **nucleophilic substitution**, a reaction that replaces the halogen of an alkyl halide with another group, producing alcohols, ethers, amines, and many other compounds. To obtain the desired product, you must also understand the **elimination** reaction that competes under the same conditions.

A species that donates an electron pair to attack a carbon bearing a partial positive charge (such as OH⁻ or CN⁻) is called a **nucleophile**, and a group that departs (such as Br⁻ or I⁻) is called a **leaving group**. There are two substitution mechanisms. In **SN2**, the nucleophile attacks from the **opposite side** of the leaving group, and the process occurs in a single concerted step. The rate is $= k[\text{기질}][\text{친핵체}]$ (second order), and if there is a stereocenter, its configuration is **inverted**. In **SN1**, the leaving group departs first, producing a **carbocation** intermediate (the slow step), and the nucleophile then attaches from either side. The rate is $= k[\text{기질}]$ (first order), and if there is a stereocenter, it becomes **racemized**.

Which mechanism predominates depends largely on the structure of the substrate. SN2 requires attack from the back, so the order is **methyl > primary > secondary**, and tertiary carbons almost never react because of steric hindrance. SN1 depends on the stability of the carbocation, so the order is **tertiary > secondary**, and it hardly occurs with methyl or primary substrates. Polar protic solvents (water, alcohols) favor SN1, while strong nucleophiles and polar aprotic solvents favor SN2.

Under strong base or at high temperature, **elimination reactions** (E1, E2) compete, in which the leaving group and a hydrogen on an adjacent carbon leave together, forming a double bond. When several adjacent hydrogens are available, the **more substituted (more stable) alkene** usually becomes the major product (Zaitsev's rule). For a tertiary halide with a strong base, elimination predominates.

How can we tell that a reaction has occurred? **Infrared (IR) spectroscopy** reveals functional groups from the wavenumbers (cm⁻¹) of light absorbed by bond vibrations. O–H gives a broad band at about 3200–3550 cm⁻¹, C=O a strong, sharp band at about 1700 cm⁻¹, C≡N a band at about 2250 cm⁻¹, and C–H bands at about 2850–3000 cm⁻¹. If a bromoalkane has been converted to an alcohol, a new broad O–H band near 3300 cm⁻¹ should appear.

Limitation: The distinctions among SN1, SN2, E1, and E2 are idealized extremes. Secondary substrates may follow several pathways mixed together, depending on the conditions. Also, IR tells us only the **presence** of functional groups and cannot determine the overall structure of a molecule; for structure determination, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) and mass spectrometry are used together.

examples.title: Predicting the Mechanism
body: Given: (a) bromomethane + NaOH in acetone solvent; (b) 2-bromo-2-methylpropane + water.
Step 1: (a) is a methyl substrate with a strong nucleophile → SN2; the rate is proportional to both concentrations.
Step 2: (b) is a tertiary substrate with a weak nucleophile in a protic solvent → SN1. It proceeds through a tertiary carbocation, so the rate depends only on the substrate concentration.

Step 1: The spectrum before the reaction shows a broad O–H band near 3300 cm⁻¹.
Step 2: After the reaction, the O–H band should disappear and a strong C=O band should appear near 1715 cm⁻¹. Both changes must be observed to conclude that the reaction went to completion.

If a strong base is present, elimination, which removes a hydrogen, also becomes dominant.

chem-19.title: Comprehensive Problem Solving: Analysis of the Ammonia Synthesis Process
explain: The first lesson of the capstone analyzes a representative chemical process, **ammonia synthesis** (the Haber–Bosch process), from the three perspectives of thermodynamics, equilibrium, and kinetics at the same time. As the basis of fertilizer production, this process is a classic example of how one compromises when thermodynamically favorable conditions and kinetically favorable conditions conflict.

**Step 1 (thermodynamics)**: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, $\Delta H^\circ = -92$ kJ, $\Delta S^\circ = -199$ J/K (4 mol of gas → 2 mol). At 25°C, $\Delta G^\circ = -92 + 298 \times 0.199 \approx -32.7$ kJ, so the reaction is spontaneous. However, because $\Delta H < 0$ and $\Delta S < 0$, it becomes **unfavorable at high temperatures**. The temperature at which $\Delta G^\circ = 0$ is about $92000/199 \approx 462$ K (about 190°C).

**Step 2 (equilibrium)**: Since $\ln K = -\Delta G^\circ/RT$, at 25°C $K \approx e^{13.2} \approx 5 \times 10^5$, strongly favoring the product side. At 450°C, $\Delta G^\circ$ becomes positive, and $K$ becomes much smaller than 1 (in practice, on the order of $10^{-5}$). According to Le Châtelier's principle, the equilibrium yield is raised by **high pressure** (toward the side with fewer moles of gas) and by **removing the product** (cooling the ammonia so that it is removed as a liquid).

**Step 3 (kinetics)**: The N≡N triple bond is very strong and has a large activation energy. At 25°C, even though $K$ is large, the reaction practically does not occur. According to the Arrhenius equation, raising the temperature increases the rate sharply, but, as seen in Step 2, the equilibrium yield falls. Iron-based **catalysts** lower the activation energy and give a sufficient rate at a moderate temperature. A catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium.

**Step 4 (compromise)**: The actual process uses about 400–450°C, 150–300 atm, an iron catalyst, and a design that **recycles unreacted gases**. The conversion in a single pass is only about 15%, but by removing the NH₃ produced and recirculating the remaining N₂ and H₂, the overall conversion is raised. The limit of equilibrium is overcome through process design.

**Critique**: This analysis assumed that $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$ are independent of temperature, and that gases behave as ideal gases at high pressure. In an actual design, the errors from these two assumptions, the energy cost of compression, and the carbon dioxide emitted by the process that makes the hydrogen feedstock must also be weighed together. The "optimum" of a chemical process is not determined by chemistry alone.

examples.title: The Dual Effect of Temperature
body: Given: the same process compared at 400°C and 500°C.
Step 1 (equilibrium): Because the reaction is exothermic, $K$ is smaller at 500°C. The equilibrium yield is lower.
Step 2 (rate): Since $E_a$ is large, the rate constant at 500°C is much larger, and equilibrium is reached faster. Which is better depends on the goal of 'production per unit time.'

examples.title: The Effect of Recycling
body: Given: a conversion of 15% per pass, assuming all unreacted gas is recycled.

Interpretation: Fresh feedstock ends up passing through the reactor many times and becomes almost entirely ammonia. However, inert gases such as argon in the recycled gas accumulate, so some of it must be continuously removed (purged). This loss ultimately sets the limit on the actual overall yield.

chem-20.title: Capstone: Reaction Path Design and Critique
explain: The final task is to **pick one chemical change, analyze it from four perspectives (thermodynamics, equilibrium, kinetics, and structure), design its conditions, and critique that design**. The subject may be a hypothetical reaction or an everyday chemical change, such as baking bread, rust formation, battery discharge, or making vinegar.

Analytical framework: ① **Thermodynamics**: Is it exothermic or endothermic? Does entropy increase? In what temperature range is it spontaneous? ② **Equilibrium**: Is K large or small? Which conditions raise the yield? ③ **Kinetics**: Is the activation energy large? Is a catalyst needed? What is the rate-determining step? ④ **Structure**: Which bonds break and which form? Does stereochemistry matter? Which spectroscopic method would confirm the product?

In the design, state the **trade-offs** explicitly. Raising the temperature speeds up the reaction but lowers the yield of an exothermic reaction. Raising the pressure raises the yield but costs equipment and energy. A good design report shows, in numbers, what was gained and what was given up.

Questions for critique: Are the assumptions of ideal gases and ideal solutions valid? How large could the error be from treating $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ as independent of temperature? Are there side reactions (unwanted products)? What are the safety and environmental costs? This lesson does not prescribe experimental procedures. Actual chemical experiments must be carried out only in appropriate facilities and under supervision.
This lesson's task is not graded. The submitted writing is stored only on this device and can be viewed again under 'What I wrote' in 'My Progress.'

examples.title: Model Structure: Rusting of Iron
body: Thermodynamics: 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃ is strongly exothermic and has a large negative $\Delta G^\circ$, so it is spontaneous. Gas is consumed, so $\Delta S < 0$, but $\Delta H$ dominates.
Kinetics: In dry air it is very slow, but in the presence of water and an electrolyte (salt), it is accelerated by an electrochemical pathway (local cells).
Design: Block oxygen and water by painting or plating, or attach zinc, which is more easily oxidized, as a sacrificial electrode (standard reduction potentials Zn −0.76 V < Fe −0.44 V).
Critique: Comparing standard potentials refers to standard conditions, and the actual corrosion rate depends strongly on humidity, temperature, and salinity.

examples.title: Model Structure: Ester Synthesis (a Hypothetical Fragrance)
body: Equilibrium: carboxylic acid + alcohol ⇌ ester + water, with $K \approx 4$, which is not very large.
Design: Add one reactant in excess and remove the water to raise the yield by Le Châtelier's principle. Use an acid catalyst to increase the rate.
Confirmation: In the IR spectrum, check whether the broad O–H band decreases and an ester C=O band appears near 1740 cm⁻¹.

checks.model: I will analyze the Maillard reaction that occurs when baking bread. In this reaction, the effect of oven temperature on the rate matters more than the enthalpy change of the reaction itself. It is a multi-step reaction that proceeds quickly at high temperatures once the activation energy is overcome. It can be spontaneous even at room temperature but is very slow. When there is a lot of moisture, the temperature is held near 100°C and the reaction is sluggish, so the surface browns faster as it dries. It is an example in which the rate, rather than the equilibrium, determines the result.
